title: light passed hand to hand
hook: a flame on a plate, moved in circles, then carried around the room

segments.voice: Yesterday: namaste, I bow to you, and the bow that touches an elder's feet. Today, the flame that comes around on a plate.

Evening at a temple. Or the steps down to a river, as dusk comes in. Or a living room, when the lamp comes out. A small flame sits on a metal plate, and someone moves it in slow circles in front of the shrine. A bell rings. People sing. Then the plate is carried around the room, and one by one, people pass their hands over the flame and bring their palms to their eyes and forehead. It takes a few minutes, start to finish. Today's word is that flame, and what happens when it leaves the shrine.
screen: `A FLAME ON A PLATE.` → `SLOW CIRCLES. A BELL.` → `THEN IT COMES TO THE PEOPLE.`

segments.voice: Arti. The waving of a lamp; the offering of light. After the flowers and food are offered, the lamp is circled before the image of God, and a song is sung. The best known begins: Om jai jagadish hare. Victory to you, lord of the world. An old Hindu text has a line that helps with what the lamp might mean: the sun doesn't shine there, nor the moon and stars, let alone this little fire; everything shines after that one shining. So a small flame held up before God is light offered back to where light comes from. Then the flame leaves the shrine and goes out to the people. Each person draws its warmth toward their face. The same small fire touches every face in the room, and nobody gets more of it. Often there's one more step: prasad. Food or sweets offered before God, then handed out. The sweet you got after temple as a kid was that: an offering, given back as a blessing.
screen: `ARTI — THE OFFERING OF LIGHT` · `EVERYTHING SHINES AFTER THAT ONE` · `THE SAME FIRE TOUCHES EVERY FACE` · `PRASAD — GIVEN BACK AS A BLESSING`

segments.voice: One breath with the bell. If there's a candle or a lamp near you, look at it; any light in the room will do. Cup your hands toward it, as if gathering warmth, and bring them to your eyes and forehead. Then bring one person to mind and turn your cupped hands toward them, as if passing the plate.
Arti. The offering of light, and then the light shared with everyone. Fifth word.
Your line: light passed hand to hand. Next time the plate comes around, you'll know what you're doing. Day five.

howItsDone: Arti is performed in temples and homes, often in the morning and evening: a lamp is waved before the image of God while a bell rings and a song is sung, and then the flame is brought to each person, who passes their hands over it and touches their eyes and forehead.

story.title: the song everyone knows
story.text: The most famous arti song isn't ancient at all. Om jai jagadish hare was written around 1870 by a Punjabi scholar named Shardha Ram Phillauri. He probably never imagined it would end up sung in living rooms from Delhi to Dallas, by families who assume it's thousands of years old.
story.source: Om jai jagadish hare, attributed to Shardha Ram Phillauri (c. 1870)

Katha 2.2.15 (5.15 in some numberings): na tatra suryo bhati na chandra-tarakam nema vidyuto bhanti kuto 'yam agnih / tam eva bhantam anubhati sarvam tasya bhasa sarvam idam vibhati. Paraphrased in English; transliteration quoted. Confirm.
'Some teachers read it as light offered back to where light comes from' links arti to this verse as an interpretation, not a textual claim. Confirm it's acceptable.

'Om jai jagadish hare' glossed as 'victory to you, lord of the world' (hare as a vocative of Hari); confirm the gloss. The song is commonly attributed to Shardha Ram Phillauri (nineteenth century); attribution left out of the voice.
